2. Calling Parent Class Constructor

The super() keyword can be used in a subclass constructor to explicitly invoke the constructor of its immediate parent class. This must be the first statement in the subclass constructor.

class Vehicle {
  String brand;
  Vehicle(String brand) {
    this.brand = brand;
  }
}

class Car extends Vehicle {
  Car(String brand) {
    super(brand); // Calls parent constructor
  }
}

codeExamples.title: Accessing Overridden Parent Method
Invoking Parent Constructor with Parameters
Using super to Access Parent Field

keyTakeaways: The super keyword refers to the immediate parent class instance.
Use super.methodName() to call an overridden method from the parent class.
Use super() to invoke the parent class constructor—must be the first line in the subclass constructor.
super can also access parent class fields, especially when they are shadowed by subclass fields.
If a subclass constructor does not explicitly call super(), Java automatically inserts a call to the no-argument parent constructor.
Attempting to use super() after other statements in a constructor results in a compile-time error.

inherit_chain.title: Understanding Inheritance Chains in Java
inherit_chain.overview: Students will learn how inheritance chains work in Java, including multilevel and hierarchical inheritance. They'll understand constructor execution order, superclass-subclass relationships, and how to effectively reuse code through inheritance.
inherit_chain.keyConceptsHtml:
1. Multilevel Inheritance

Multilevel inheritance occurs when a class extends another class that itself extends another class, forming a chain. When an object of the most derived class is created, constructors are called from the topmost superclass down to the subclass.

class Vehicle {
    Vehicle() {
        System.out.println("This is a Vehicle");
    }
}

class FourWheeler extends Vehicle {
    FourWheeler() {
        System.out.println("4 Wheeler Vehicles");
    }
}

class Car extends FourWheeler {
    Car() {
        System.out.println("This 4 Wheeler Vehicle is a Car");
    }
}

2. Hierarchical Inheritance

Hierarchical inheritance occurs when multiple subclasses inherit from a single superclass. Each subclass shares the common features of the superclass but can also define their own unique behavior.

public class CardCollection {
    protected String label;
    public CardCollection(String label) {
        this.label = label;
    }
}

public class Deck extends CardCollection {
    public Deck(String label) {
        super(label);
        for (int suit = 0; suit <= 3; suit++) {
            for (int rank = 1; rank <= 13; rank++) {
                // addCard(new Card(rank, suit));
            }
        }
    }
}

3. Constructor Chaining in Inheritance

In Java, when a subclass object is instantiated, the constructor of its immediate superclass is automatically invoked (via an implicit or explicit super() call), which in turn invokes its superclass constructor, continuing up to Object. This ensures proper initialization of inherited state.

codeExamples.title: Multilevel Inheritance with Constructor Execution
Hierarchical Inheritance with Shared Superclass
Explicit Superclass Constructor Call

keyTakeaways: In multilevel inheritance, constructors execute from the topmost superclass down to the most derived subclass.
Every class in Java implicitly inherits from the Object class if no explicit superclass is defined.
The 'extends' keyword is used to create a subclass that inherits fields and methods from a superclass.
Hierarchical inheritance allows multiple classes to share common functionality from one parent class.
Use the 'super()' keyword to explicitly invoke a superclass constructor—this must be the first statement in the subclass constructor.
Inheritance promotes code reusability and establishes an 'is-a' relationship between classes (e.g., a Car is a FourWheeler).

inherit_types.title: Types of Inheritance in Java
inherit_types.overview: Students will learn about the different types of inheritance supported in Java, including single, multilevel, and hierarchical inheritance. They will also understand why multiple and hybrid inheritance are not directly supported through classes but can be achieved using interfaces.
inherit_types.keyConceptsHtml:
1. Single Inheritance

In single inheritance, a subclass inherits from only one superclass. This is the most common and straightforward form of inheritance in Java.

class Vehicle {
    Vehicle() {
        System.out.println("This is a Vehicle");
    }
}

class Car extends Vehicle {
    Car() {
        System.out.println("This Vehicle is Car");
    }
}

2. Multilevel Inheritance

In multilevel inheritance, a class is derived from a subclass, forming a chain of inheritance. For example, Class C extends Class B, which extends Class A.

class Animal {
    void eat() { System.out.println("Animal eats"); }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    void bark() { System.out.println("Dog barks"); }
}

class Puppy extends Dog {
    void weep() { System.out.println("Puppy weeps"); }
}

3. Hierarchical Inheritance

In hierarchical inheritance, multiple subclasses inherit from a single superclass. This allows code reuse across several related classes.

class Shape {
    void draw() { System.out.println("Drawing a shape"); }
}

class Circle extends Shape {
    void drawCircle() { System.out.println("Drawing a circle"); }
}

class Rectangle extends Shape {
    void drawRect() { System.out.println("Drawing a rectangle"); }
}

4. Multiple Inheritance (via Interfaces)

Java does not support multiple inheritance with classes to avoid ambiguity (e.g., the diamond problem). However, a class can implement multiple interfaces to achieve similar functionality.

interface Flyable {
    void fly();
}

interface Swimmable {
    void swim();
}

class Duck implements Flyable, Swimmable {
    public void fly() { System.out.println("Duck is flying"); }
    public void swim() { System.out.println("Duck is swimming"); }
}

5. Hybrid Inheritance

Hybrid inheritance is a combination of two or more types of inheritance. Since Java doesn’t support multiple inheritance with classes, hybrid inheritance is implemented using a mix of classes and interfaces.

class LivingBeing {
    void breathe() { System.out.println("Breathing..."); }
}

interface Movable {
    void move();
}

interface Speakable {
    void speak();
}

class Human extends LivingBeing implements Movable, Speakable {
    public void move() { System.out.println("Human is walking"); }
    public void speak() { System.out.println("Human is speaking"); }
}

codeExamples.title: Single Inheritance Example
Multilevel Inheritance Example
Hierarchical Inheritance with Method Overriding

keyTakeaways: Java supports single, multilevel, and hierarchical inheritance using classes.
Multiple inheritance is not allowed with classes in Java to prevent ambiguity (e.g., the diamond problem).
Interfaces enable a form of multiple inheritance by allowing a class to implement multiple interfaces.
Hybrid inheritance can be achieved in Java by combining class inheritance with interface implementation.
Inheritance promotes code reusability and establishes an 'is-a' relationship between classes.
Method overriding in inherited classes allows polymorphic behavior, a core principle of object-oriented programming.

poly_overload.title: Compile-time Polymorphism in Java
poly_overload.overview: Students will learn how compile-time polymorphism—also known as method overloading—enables multiple methods with the same name but different parameters within a single class. This lesson covers its syntax, rules, practical examples, and key benefits in Java programming.
poly_overload.keyConceptsHtml:
1. What is Compile-Time Polymorphism?

Compile-time polymorphism, or static polymorphism, occurs when multiple methods in the same class share the same name but differ in their parameter lists (number, type, or order of parameters). The correct method is resolved by the compiler during compilation, not at runtime.

2. Rules for Method Overloading

To overload a method in Java, you must change the method signature. This means changing the number of parameters, the data types of parameters, or the order of different-type parameters. Return type alone cannot differentiate overloaded methods.

class Calculator {
    int add(int a, int b) {
        return a + b;
    }
    
    double add(double a, double b) {
        return a + b;
    }
    
    int add(int a, int b, int c) {
        return a + b + c;
    }
}

3. Operator Overloading in Java

Unlike some other languages (e.g., C++), Java does not support user-defined operator overloading. The only built-in operator overloading in Java is the '+' operator for String concatenation.

codeExamples.title: Basic Method Overloading Example
Overloading with Different Parameter Types
Overloading Based on Parameter Order

keyTakeaways: Compile-time polymorphism is achieved through method overloading in Java.
Overloaded methods must differ in their parameter list—either in number, type, or order of parameters.
Return type alone is not sufficient to distinguish overloaded methods.
Method resolution for overloading happens at compile time, improving performance compared to runtime polymorphism.
Java does not support user-defined operator overloading; only the '+' operator is overloaded for String concatenation.
Method overloading promotes code readability and reusability by allowing logically similar operations to share a common method name.

poly_override.title: Runtime Polymorphism in Java
poly_override.overview: In this lesson, students will learn how Java enables a single method call to produce different behaviors based on the actual object type at runtime. This is achieved through method overriding and dynamic method dispatch, core features of object-oriented programming.
poly_override.keyConceptsHtml:
1. Multiple Behaviors

Runtime polymorphism allows the same method to behave differently depending on the object that invokes it. This is possible because Java uses the actual object type—not the reference type—to determine which method implementation to execute.

2. Method Overriding

A subclass can provide a specific implementation of a method already defined in its parent class. The method signature (name, parameters, and return type) must match exactly, and the access modifier cannot be more restrictive.

class Animal {
    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Animal makes a sound");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    @Override
    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Dog barks");
    }
}

3. Runtime Decision

Java determines which overridden method to call at runtime based on the actual object type, not the reference variable type. This mechanism is known as dynamic method dispatch.

codeExamples.title: Basic Runtime Polymorphism Example
Polymorphic Array and Loop
Polymorphism with Method Parameters

keyTakeaways: Runtime polymorphism allows a single method call to invoke different implementations based on the actual object type at runtime.
Method overriding is essential for runtime polymorphism—subclasses must redefine parent methods with identical signatures.
The reference type determines what methods can be called, but the object type determines which implementation is executed.
Dynamic method dispatch is the mechanism Java uses to resolve overridden method calls during program execution.
Polymorphism promotes code reusability and simplifies maintenance by enabling generic code that works with multiple subclasses.
While powerful, excessive use of polymorphism can reduce code readability and introduce minor performance overhead due to runtime resolution.

poly_dynamic.title: Dynamic Method Dispatch in Java
poly_dynamic.overview: Students will learn how Java resolves method calls at runtime using dynamic method dispatch, a core mechanism of runtime polymorphism achieved through method overriding. This enables flexible and extensible object-oriented designs by allowing subclasses to provide specific implementations of inherited methods.
poly_dynamic.keyConceptsHtml:
1. Runtime Polymorphism

Runtime polymorphism, also known as dynamic method dispatch, is the process where a call to an overridden method is resolved at runtime rather than compile time. This allows Java to decide which version of a method (from superclass or subclass) to execute based on the actual object type.

2. Method Overriding

Method overriding occurs when a subclass provides a specific implementation of a method already defined in its superclass. The method signature (name, parameters, return type) must be identical, and the access modifier cannot be more restrictive. Dynamic method dispatch uses this feature to invoke the correct method at runtime.

class Animal {
    void speak() {
        System.out.println("Animal speaks");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    @Override
    void speak() {
        System.out.println("Dog barks");
    }
}

codeExamples.title: Basic Dynamic Method Dispatch
Multiple Subclasses with Overridden Methods
Dynamic Dispatch in Collections

keyTakeaways: Dynamic method dispatch enables runtime polymorphism by resolving overridden method calls based on the actual object type, not the reference type.
Method overriding requires the subclass method to have the same name, parameters, and return type as the superclass method.
The JVM determines which overridden method to invoke at runtime by examining the actual instance type, not the declared reference type.
Upcasting (assigning a subclass object to a superclass reference) is commonly used to leverage dynamic method dispatch.
Static methods cannot be overridden and are not subject to dynamic dispatch—they are bound at compile time.
Using dynamic method dispatch promotes code reusability, maintainability, and clean hierarchical design in object-oriented Java programs.

poly_casting.title: Type Casting and instanceof in Java
poly_casting.overview: Students will learn how to convert between data types using widening and narrowing casting, and how to safely check object types at runtime using the instanceof operator. This includes understanding when casting is automatic versus when it must be explicit, and how to avoid ClassCastException.
poly_casting.keyConceptsHtml:
1. Widening Casting (Automatic)

Widening casting occurs when a smaller data type is converted to a larger one. This is done automatically by Java because no data loss occurs.

int myInt = 9;
double myDouble = myInt; // Automatic casting: int to double

2. Narrowing Casting (Manual)

Narrowing casting converts a larger data type to a smaller one and must be done explicitly using parentheses. This can result in data loss or precision issues.

double myDouble = 9.78;
int myInt = (int) myDouble; // Manual casting: double to int

3. instanceof Operator

The instanceof operator checks whether an object is an instance of a specific class or implements a particular interface. It returns true if the object matches the type, and false otherwise—helping prevent ClassCastException during downcasting.

Object obj = new String("Hello");
if (obj instanceof String) {
    String str = (String) obj; // Safe cast
}

codeExamples.title: Widening Casting Example
Narrowing Casting Example
Using instanceof for Safe Downcasting

keyTakeaways: Widening casting (e.g., int to double) is automatic and safe because it doesn’t lose data.
Narrowing casting (e.g., double to int) requires explicit syntax and may result in data loss or truncation.
Always use the instanceof operator before downcasting to avoid ClassCastException at runtime.
The instanceof operator returns false if the object is null, making it safe for null checks.
Type casting applies to both primitive types and object references, but rules differ between them.
In object-oriented contexts, upcasting is implicit (e.g., subclass to superclass), while downcasting must be explicit and verified.

interface_basics.title: Java Interface Basics
interface_basics.overview: Students will learn how to define and implement interfaces in Java, understand their role in achieving abstraction and multiple inheritance, and apply them in practical programming scenarios.
interface_basics.keyConceptsHtml:
1. What is an Interface?

An interface in Java is a reference type that can contain only constants, method signatures, default methods, static methods, and nested types. It cannot contain method implementations (except for default and static methods). Interfaces are used to specify a contract for classes to follow.

interface Animal {
    void makeSound();
}

2. Implementing an Interface

A class implements an interface using the implements keyword and must provide concrete implementations for all abstract methods declared in the interface. A class can implement multiple interfaces.

class Dog implements Animal {
    public void makeSound() {
        System.out.println("Woof!");
    }
}

3. Multiple Inheritance with Interfaces

Unlike classes, Java allows a class to implement multiple interfaces, enabling a form of multiple inheritance of type. This helps design flexible and modular systems.

interface Swimmable {
    void swim();
}

class Duck implements Animal, Swimmable {
    public void makeSound() {
        System.out.println("Quack!");
    }
    public void swim() {
        System.out.println("Duck is swimming.");
    }
}

codeExamples.title: Basic Interface Definition and Implementation
Class Implementing Multiple Interfaces
Using Interface as a Reference Type

keyTakeaways: An interface defines a contract that implementing classes must fulfill by providing concrete implementations of all abstract methods.
Interfaces support multiple inheritance in Java, allowing a class to implement more than one interface.
Variables in an interface are implicitly public, static, and final—meaning they are constants.
Methods in an interface are by default public and abstract (unless marked as default or static).
Interfaces enable polymorphism by allowing objects of different classes to be treated uniformly through a common interface type.
Using interfaces promotes loose coupling and makes code more modular, testable, and maintainable.

interface_implement.title: Implementing Interfaces in Java
interface_implement.overview: Students will learn how to define and implement interfaces in Java, understand their role in achieving abstraction and multiple inheritance, and apply them to enforce method contracts across classes.
interface_implement.keyConceptsHtml:
1. What is an Interface?

An interface in Java is a reference type that defines a contract of abstract methods. Any class that implements the interface must provide concrete implementations for all its methods. Interfaces enable abstraction and support multiple inheritance since a class can implement multiple interfaces.

interface Drawable {
    void draw();
}

2. Implementing a Single Interface

A class uses the implements keyword to fulfill the contract defined by an interface. It must override all abstract methods declared in the interface.

class Circle implements Drawable {
    public void draw() {
        System.out.println("Drawing a circle");
    }
}

3. Implementing Multiple Interfaces

Java allows a class to implement more than one interface by listing them after the implements keyword, separated by commas. This is Java’s way of supporting multiple inheritance of type.

interface Resizable {
    void resize();
}

class Rectangle implements Drawable, Resizable {
    public void draw() {
        System.out.println("Drawing a rectangle");
    }
    
    public void resize() {
        System.out.println("Resizing rectangle");
    }
}

codeExamples.title: Basic Interface Implementation
Multiple Interface Implementation
Using Interfaces for Polymorphism

keyTakeaways: An interface defines a contract of method signatures that implementing classes must fulfill.
All methods in an interface are implicitly public and abstract (unless they are default or static methods introduced in Java 8+).
A class implements an interface using the 'implements' keyword and must provide concrete implementations for all abstract methods.
Java supports multiple inheritance of type through interfaces—a class can implement multiple interfaces separated by commas.
Interfaces enable polymorphism, allowing objects of different classes to be treated uniformly if they implement the same interface.
Variables declared in an interface are automatically public, static, and final—effectively constants.

interface_default.title: Default Methods in Interfaces
interface_default.overview: Students will learn how to define and use default methods in Java interfaces, introduced in JDK 8. This feature allows interfaces to provide method implementations without breaking existing implementations, enabling backward compatibility and code reuse.
interface_default.keyConceptsHtml:
1. What Are Default Methods?

Default methods allow interfaces to provide concrete method implementations using the default keyword. They are public by default and can be overridden by implementing classes.

interface Vehicle {
    default void start() {
        System.out.println("Vehicle is starting...");
    }
}

2. Multiple Inheritance and Default Methods

When a class implements multiple interfaces that have default methods with the same signature, the class must override the method to resolve ambiguity. This prevents the 'diamond problem'.

interface A {
    default void greet() { System.out.println("Hello from A"); }
}

interface B {
    default void greet() { System.out.println("Hello from B"); }
}

class C implements A, B {
    public void greet() {
        A.super.greet(); // Explicitly call A's version
    }
}

3. Evolution of Interfaces with Default Methods

Default methods enable adding new functionality to existing interfaces without requiring all implementing classes to be modified—crucial for library evolution like the Java Collections Framework.

codeExamples.title: Basic Default Method Implementation
Overriding a Default Method
Resolving Conflicts with Multiple Interfaces

keyTakeaways: Default methods in interfaces are declared with the 'default' keyword and provide a concrete implementation.
All interface members, including default methods, are public by default—no access modifiers are needed.
Classes implementing an interface may choose to override a default method or inherit it as-is.
If a class implements multiple interfaces with conflicting default methods, it must override the method to resolve ambiguity.
Default methods were introduced in Java 8 to support interface evolution without breaking existing code.
Interfaces can also contain static methods (since Java 8) and private methods (since Java 9) to support helper logic for default methods.

interface_functional.title: Functional Interfaces in Java
interface_functional.overview: Students will learn what functional interfaces are, how to define and use them with lambda expressions and method references, and understand the role of the @FunctionalInterface annotation. They will also explore practical examples demonstrating their use in real-world Java programming.
interface_functional.keyConceptsHtml:
1. What is a Functional Interface?

A functional interface is an interface that contains exactly one abstract method. It may include any number of default or static methods, but only one unimplemented method. This makes it compatible with lambda expressions.

@FunctionalInterface
public interface Calculator {
    int compute(int x, int y);
}

2. Using Lambda Expressions with Functional Interfaces

Lambda expressions provide a concise way to implement the single abstract method of a functional interface without writing a full class. This enables cleaner, more readable code for behaviors like event handling or data processing.

Calculator add = (a, b) -> a + b;
System.out.println(add.compute(5, 3)); // Output: 8

3. Built-in Functional Interfaces

Java provides several built-in functional interfaces in the java.util.function package, such as Predicate, Function, Consumer, and Supplier. These reduce the need to create custom interfaces for common operations.

import java.util.function.Predicate;

Predicate isEmpty = str -> str.isEmpty();
System.out.println(isEmpty.test("")); // true

The @FunctionalInterface annotation is optional but recommended—it helps the compiler enforce the single abstract method rule.
Lambda expressions provide a clean syntax to implement functional interfaces inline without defining a separate class.
Method references (e.g., ClassName::methodName) can be used wherever a lambda expression matches a functional interface’s method signature.
Java’s java.util.function package includes commonly used functional interfaces like Predicate, Function, Consumer, and Supplier.
Functional interfaces enable functional programming patterns in Java, making code more expressive and easier to parallelize (e.g., with Streams).

lambda_syntax.title: Lambda Expressions in Java
lambda_syntax.overview: Students will learn how to use lambda expressions to write concise and functional-style code in Java. They will understand the syntax, use cases with functional interfaces, and how lambdas simplify common programming tasks like sorting and event handling.
lambda_syntax.keyConceptsHtml:
1. What is a Lambda Expression?

A lambda expression is a concise way to represent an anonymous function (a method without a name) that can be passed as an argument or stored in a variable. It requires a functional interface—any interface with exactly one abstract method.

// Functional interface
@FunctionalInterface
interface MathOperation {
    int operate(int a, int b);
}

// Lambda expression implementing the interface
MathOperation add = (a, b) -> a + b;

2. Syntax and Structure

Lambda expressions follow the syntax: (parameters) -> expression or (parameters) -> { statements; }. Parentheses around parameters can be omitted if there's only one parameter, and curly braces are optional for single-expression bodies.

// Single parameter, no parentheses
Predicate isEmpty = s -> s.isEmpty();

// Multiple parameters, block body
BiFunction multiply = (x, y) -> {
    System.out.println("Multiplying " + x + " and " + y);
    return x * y;
};

3. Common Use Cases

Lambdas are frequently used with the Java Collections Framework (e.g., forEach, stream().filter()) and for event handling in GUI applications. They eliminate boilerplate code associated with anonymous inner classes.

List names = Arrays.asList("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie");
names.forEach(name -> System.out.println(name));

// Filtering with stream
List longNames = names.stream()
    .filter(s -> s.length() > 4)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

A functional interface must have exactly one abstract method; use @FunctionalInterface to enforce this.
Lambdas enable functional programming patterns in Java, especially when working with streams and collections.
Parameter types in lambdas can often be inferred by the compiler, reducing verbosity.
Use curly braces {} in the lambda body when multiple statements are needed; otherwise, a single expression suffices.
Common standard functional interfaces include Predicate, Function, Consumer, and Supplier from java.util.function.

recursion_basics.title: Recursion Fundamentals in Java
recursion_basics.overview: Students will learn how recursion works in Java by understanding the core principles of recursive methods, including base cases and recursive calls. They will explore practical examples such as computing factorials and summing number ranges using self-invoking functions.
recursion_basics.keyConceptsHtml:
1. What is Recursion?

Recursion is a programming technique where a method calls itself to solve a smaller instance of the same problem. It’s an alternative to iterative loops and is especially useful for problems that can be broken down into similar subproblems.

public static void countDown(int n) {
    if (n <= 0) {
        System.out.println("Done!");
    } else {
        System.out.println(n);
        countDown(n - 1); // recursive call
    }
}

2. Base Case and Recursive Case

Every recursive method must have a base case—a condition that stops further recursion—to prevent infinite loops. The recursive case is where the method calls itself with modified arguments, moving closer to the base case.

public static int factorial(int n) {
    if (n == 0 || n == 1) { // base case
        return 1;
    } else {
        return n * factorial(n - 1); // recursive case
    }
}

3. Recursion vs. Iteration

While loops and for-loops provide iterative solutions, recursion offers a more elegant and readable approach for certain problems like tree traversals or mathematical sequences. However, recursion uses more memory due to the call stack, so it should be used thoughtfully.

Recursion can simplify code for problems with self-similar structure, such as mathematical sequences or tree navigation.

recursion_vs_iterative.title: Recursion vs Iteration in Java
recursion_vs_iterative.overview: Students will learn the fundamental differences between recursive and iterative approaches in Java, understand when to use each, and implement common algorithms using both techniques. Emphasis is placed on base cases, method calls, and loop structures.
recursion_vs_iterative.keyConceptsHtml:
1. Recursive Methods

A recursive method solves a problem by calling itself with modified arguments until it reaches a base case. This approach often leads to cleaner, more readable code for problems that have self-similar subproblems.

public static int factorial(int n) {
    if (n == 0 || n == 1) { // base case
        return 1;
    }
    return n * factorial(n - 1); // recursive call
}

2. Iterative Methods

An iterative method uses loops (for, while, or do-while) to repeat steps until a condition is met. It typically uses less memory than recursion because it avoids repeated method calls on the call stack.

public static int factorialIterative(int n) {
    int result = 1;
    for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) {
        result *= i;
    }
    return result;
}

3. Base Case and Termination

Every recursive method must have at least one base case—a condition that stops further recursive calls. Without it, the method will cause a StackOverflowError due to infinite recursion.

keyTakeaways: Recursive methods must always include a base case to prevent infinite recursion and stack overflow errors.
Iteration uses loops and generally consumes less memory than recursion because it doesn’t add new frames to the call stack.
Recursion often provides more elegant and concise solutions for problems with self-similar structure, such as tree traversals or mathematical sequences.
Both recursion and iteration can solve the same problems, but performance and readability may differ significantly.
The factorial function is a classic example used to demonstrate both recursive and iterative approaches in Java.
Understanding when to choose recursion over iteration (or vice versa) is key to writing efficient and maintainable Java code.

recursion_patterns.title: Recursive Patterns and Techniques in Java
recursion_patterns.overview: Students will learn how to design and implement recursive methods in Java, understand the importance of base cases, and recognize common recursive patterns such as computation on the way down, on the way up, or both. This material emphasizes practical problem-solving using recursion instead of iteration.
recursion_patterns.keyConceptsHtml:
1. What is Recursion?

A recursive method is one that calls itself with modified arguments to solve a smaller instance of the same problem. Every recursive method must have at least one base case to prevent infinite recursion.

public static int factorial(int n) {
    if (n == 0) { // base case
        return 1;
    }
    return n * factorial(n - 1); // recursive call
}

2. Base Case and Recursive Case

The base case stops the recursion and returns a result without further self-calls. The recursive case reduces the problem toward the base case by calling the method again with a simpler input.

3. Computation Direction in Recursion

Recursive methods can perform work before the recursive call (on the way down), after the recursive call (on the way up), or both. This affects when values are processed and combined.

Computation performed before the recursive call happens 'on the way down'; computation after happens 'on the way up'.

revision_comprehensive.title: Comprehensive Java Review: Core Concepts and Best Practices
revision_comprehensive.overview: This review covers essential Java programming concepts including encapsulation, getter/setter methods, class design, and performance considerations. Students will reinforce their understanding through practical examples and real-world usage patterns.
revision_comprehensive.keyConceptsHtml:
1. Encapsulation in Java

Encapsulation is the practice of hiding internal state and requiring all interaction to be performed through an object's methods. This promotes data integrity and modularity.

public class BankAccount {
    private double balance;

    public void deposit(double amount) {
        if (amount > 0) {
            balance += amount;
        }
    }

    public double getBalance() {
        return balance;
    }
}

2. Getter and Setter Methods

Getter and setter methods provide controlled access to private fields. While they increase code length, they allow validation, logging, or future logic changes without breaking existing code.

public class Person {
    private String name;

    public String getName() {
        return name;
    }

    public void setName(String name) {
        if (name != null && !name.trim().isEmpty()) {
            this.name = name;
        }
    }
}

3. Performance and Design Trade-offs

Using methods instead of direct field access introduces a minor performance overhead. However, in most applications, the benefits of maintainability and safety outweigh this cost. Over-restricting access may also limit extensibility in inheritance scenarios.

keyTakeaways: Encapsulation protects an object's internal state by restricting direct access to its fields.
Getter and setter methods enable validation, debugging, and future enhancements without changing client code.
While method calls have a slight performance cost, the benefits of robust, maintainable code usually justify it.
Overusing private access without considering inheritance can reduce flexibility for subclasses.
Always validate input in setter methods to maintain object integrity and prevent invalid states.
Well-designed encapsulated classes are easier to test, reuse, and integrate into larger systems.
